query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of yttrium (Y) into the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy will stabilize its oxide scale at elevated temperatures by forming nanoscale Y2O3 precipitates along the metal/oxide interface. This stabilization mitigates growth stresses and adhesion loss, thereby delaying degradation and preventing catastrophic spallation under both oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres.
generation.material_initial_state: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a single-phase FCC matrix produced via additive manufacturing, with no reactive trace element modification.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled trace addition (e.g., 0.5 at.%) of yttrium (Y) into the alloy composition prior to processing.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature exposure (approximately 900–1000°C) during extended thermal cycling in oxidizing (e.g., air/oxygen) and reducing gas environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Y2O3 precipitates that form at the interface between the existing oxide scale and the metal substrate act as pinning sites to mechanically anchor the oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: Trace Y segregates to developing oxide grain boundaries during high-temperature exposure, forming Y2O3 interfacial particles. These particles decrease cation diffusivity and relieve the buildup of growth stresses. In the absence of Y, the oxide scale accumulates tensile stresses that lead to its spallation and subsequent catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Y-modified alloy is expected to show a significant reduction in oxidation rate (potentially up to a three-order-of-magnitude decrease), enhanced oxide-scale adhesion (evidenced by higher interfacial fracture energies and critical loads), and reduced mass loss during thermal cycling. This improvement should be observable under both oxidizing and reducing conditions.
generation.baseline: The alloy without trace Y rapidly develops a less-adherent oxide scale that accumulates growth-induced stresses, leading to accelerated scale spallation, mass loss, and eventual catastrophic failure during extended high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to operate in high-temperature regimes (around 900–1000°C) in both oxidizing and reducing environments. Its efficacy may vary with the exact gas composition and thermal cycling parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The extent and uniformity of Y segregation to the oxide scale and the resulting formation of nanoscale Y2O3 precipitates in this complex HEA are uncertain and may depend on specific additive manufacturing and thermal processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: the baseline Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and a modified version with 0.5 at.% Y added. Process both sets under identical additive manufacturing conditions. Subject the samples to 100 cycles of thermal cycling at approximately 1000°C under controlled oxidizing (and separately, reducing) gas conditions.
measurements: Mass change and oxidation kinetics (to quantify oxidation rate constants)
Interfacial adhesion tests (e.g., scratch testing to determine critical load and interfacial fracture energy)
Microstructural analyses via SEM/TEM to detect and characterize Y2O3 precipitate formation at the oxide/metal interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-modified alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in oxidation rate, oxide-scale adhesion, and reduced mass loss compared to the baseline—i.e., if its performance under thermal cycling is equivalent to or worse than the Y-free alloy—the hypothesis that trace Y stabilizes the oxide scale via nanoscale Y2O3 formation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study proposes a novel synergistic design strategy to enhance the oxidation resistance of FeNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloys by integrating multi-element alloying (Cr-Co-Mn), trace Y modification, and laser-cladding-induced nanocrystallization. While the Base Alloy exhibited a mass gain of approximately 15 mg/cm2 after oxidation at 900 °C for 120 h, the addition of Cr2.5Co2.5Mn2.5 promoted the formation of a multilayered oxide scale (outer MnCr2O4/inner Al2O3), reducing the parabolic oxidation rate constant to 1.7 × 10−5 mg2·cm−4·s−1. The originality of this work lies in the coupling of compositional and microstructural engineering; further addition of 0.5 at.% Y decreased this constant to 1.7 × 10−6 mg2·cm−4·s−1—a three-order-of-magnitude reduction relative to the Base Alloy, while increasing the apparent oxidation activation energy to ~350 kJ/mol. After 100 thermal cycles at 1000 °C, the designed alloy showed a mass change of only 0.05 ± 0.02 mg/cm2, with its critical load and interfacial fracture energy reaching 78 N and 14.8 J/m2, respectively. cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 presents the mechanical stability analysis of the oxide scales. As shown in Figure 6, the cyclic oxidation results reveal pronounced differences in spallation resistance among the three alloys. The Base Alloy undergoes severe oxide-scale spallation after 100 thermal cycles at 1000 °C, resulting in substantial mass loss. The Synergy Alloy shows improved cyclic oxidation resistance, but measurable scale degradation still occurs. In contrast, the Innovation Alloy exhibits a mass change of only 0.05 ± 0.02 mg/cm2 after 100 cycles, with almost no detectable spallation, demonstrating excellent scale stability under thermal cycling. The simulated stress evolution further indicates that the oxide scale on the Innovation Alloy accumulates growth stress more slowly and can more effectively accommodate stress through local deformation and defect healing. Scratch testing confirms this enhanced interfacial stability: the critical load and interfacial fracture energy reach 78 N and 14.8 J/m2, respectively, which are substantially higher than those of the Synergy Alloy. In summary, this study developed a high-performance FeNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloy coating by revealing a triple-synergy mechanism that integrates Cr-Co-Mn multi-element alloying, trace Y modification, and laser-cladding-induced nanocrystallization. Unlike conventional oxidation-resistant alloy design strategies that mainly rely on complex alloying, this work demonstrates that the rapid solidification effect of laser cladding can generate nanocrystalline grain boundaries, which serve as fast diffusion channels for Al and Cr and promote the rapid formation of a protective MnCr2O4/Al2O3 bilayer scale. The Innovation Alloy (FeNiCuAlCr2.5Co2.5Mn2.5Y0.5) achieved a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in the parabolic oxidation rate constant, reaching 1.7 × 10−6 mg2·cm−4·s−1 at 900 °C, together with excellent scale adhesion, as indicated by a critical load of 78 N. This improvement is closely associated with the nanoscale pinning effect of approximately 35 nm Y2O3 particles at the oxide scale/alloy interface.
